I call to order this 11th informal meeting of the plenary on the question of equitable representation on an increase in the membership of the Security Council and other matters relating to the Council. My fellow co-chair and I would like to extend a warm welcome to you all, and as we approach the conclusion of the 80th session, we would like to express our sincere appreciation to all delegations for their constructive and high-level engagement throughout the process. We are grateful for the openness and willingness demonstrated by member states to engage with new ideas and proposals in a spirit of dialogue and compromise. In this regard, we wish to acknowledge and thank the African Group for presenting its model, which has contributed meaningfully to our discussions and further enriched the exchange of views amongst member states. Thank you. We also would like to thank all delegations for their active and constructive participation during the IGN Plenary on 19th of May.

As indicated in our letter dated 4 June, this meeting will serve as an opportunity for delegations to provide comments or suggestions on the revised Elements Paper. We urge delegations to be reflective of the discussions and elements of convergence and divergence that delegations have identified and articulated during this year's discussions. Delegations were invited to inscribe on the list of speakers via eDelegate, and the live link to the list of speakers was circulated to all delegations. At this stage, any delegation who wishes to be added to the existing list of speakers should inform the Secretariat table. Any delegation wishing to speak on behalf of a group States should inform the Secretariat in order to be given priority. We also encourage delegations to adhere to the time limits we have established. Statements delivered on behalf of a group of States will be limited to 5 minutes, and national statements will be limited to 3 minutes. To assist speakers with time management, we have projected the on-screen timer on the screens. Thank you. Once the list of speakers is exhausted, we will hold an interactive discussion on the revised Elements Paper in a closed meeting without webcast.

Before we begin, I would like to remind members that delegations are encouraged to email a copy of their statements to eastatements@un.org for the publication on the repository website, as well as the facilitation of interpretation. I will now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan on behalf of the Group of Four.

Thank you very much, co-chairs. I deliver this statement on behalf of G4: Brazil, Germany, India, and my own country, Japan. I thank you for preparing your elements paper, which, as firmly established, reflects the co-chair's own view of the state of discussions in the IGN. It's issued under their exclusive— under their exclusive responsibility and does not bind delegations. While reserving the G4's general position on the Elements Paper as stated above, the G4 delivers— it contains a language which is not an accurate account of the actual discussions at the IGN and would like to offer our views on the following three points at this time. The G4 will also be submitting comments in written form for your careful consideration. First, With regard to categories of membership, it is deeply regrettable that despite repeated requests from the G4, the Elements Paper continues to fail to reflect the undeniable fact that the majority of member states support the expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories. The G4's count of the number of members that have explicitly expressed support for the expansion of both categories during this 80th session has exceeded 110 member states, which is well beyond the majority threshold of 97. We are fully prepared to discuss this number. Second, the Elements Paper mentions the question of definition of permanency. However, there is no doubt— whatsoever about what permanency means in the Security Council, as Article 23 of the Charter and 80 years of uninterrupted and challenged practice clearly show. We do not see how promoting such non-existent debate will move us forward. Third, the G4 reiterates that the reform process must be led by member states. The Elements Paper refers to the so-called fixed regional seat concept as a bridging proposal. As we have indicated in the past, we do not see it as such, as it excludes the majority view in favor of the expansion in both categories. Neither do we consider that the time is ripe for proposals not coming from member states. Co-chairs, to aid in moving the reform process forward, Under the legitimacy conferred by a member states-led process, the G4 requests that the Elements Paper be faithfully revised with attribution of positions expressed by states and groups of states, including a clear majority in support for the expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan for his statement, and I now give the I give the floor to Italy on behalf of the Uniting for Consensus Group.

Distinguished co-chairs, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the UFC, a cross-regional pro-reform group composed by Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Malta, Mexico, Pakistan, the Republic of Korea, San Marino, Spain, Türkiye, and my own country, Italy. Let me begin by thanking you for convening this session and for circulating the revised Chair's Element Papers, we wish to remark that the time available for thorough review was limited. Adequate time for reflection and consultation is needed to have an enriched discussion. In the current session, the broad and growing support for a comprehensive reform of the Security Council was reaffirmed and the continued legitimacy and relevance of the IGN as the sole platform for advancing this important process were rather validated. The UFC Group remains firmly committed to a reform that makes the Security Council more representative, democratic, inclusive, accountable, transparent, effective, efficient, and responsive to today's global challenges. We wish to state clearly that we actively support comprehensive reform of the Security Council and acknowledge the urgent need for such a reform. To that And we strive to be flexible and open to ideas for how to achieve that outcome and encourage others to do the same, meaning being flexible and open. As to the draft elements paper, we appreciate your clarification that the document reflects the co-chairs' understanding of the current state of the IGN discussions and is under your authority, including on procedural aspects. On that basis, we welcome your invitation to provide comments aimed at ensuring the document faithfully captures both areas of convergence and divergence that emerged during this session of negotiations. Allow me to offer a few general observations reflecting the UFC understanding. Following the Summit of the Future in September '24, we welcomed the renewed momentum that has reinvigorated the reform process. In this regard, it is appropriate to reaffirm the guidance provided by the Pact in the Elements Paper. However, we recall that the IJN process emanated from Decision 62/557 and continues to be conducted in accordance with its key provisions, including the 5 interlinked clusters. Therefore, we caution against any formulation suggesting that the Pact for the Future constituted a so-called formal mandate for the IGFN. While Action 39 sets out clear guiding principles, these refer to those identified in the work of the IGFN and in accordance with the General Assembly Decision 62/557. While we acknowledge the encouragement to submit further reform models and the revision of already presented models, we underscore that the actual objective remains to develop a consolidated model through the reaching of convergence across the 5 clusters. We do not recall any delegations stating that, as mentioned in the draft elements paper, the development of a consolidated model constitutes an objective of the IGN per se. The overarching goal remains to forge a common vision on the most controversial issues in order to implement a reform that becomes more urgent every day. Distinguished co-chairs, regarding the elements of general convergence, the UFC continues to attach great importance to the following principles: One, the reform process must remain member-state driven. Two, the AGN is the only legitimate, inclusive and appropriate platform to pursue reform. Three, outcomes must garner the widest possible political acceptance— in line with the General Assembly Decision 62/557 and Resolution 53/30. These are the only legal sources of our mandate in the reform process. Four, given the interlinkages between the five clusters, the process must uphold the principle that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. Turning to the core principles underpinning Security Council reform, we wish to reiterate that for UFC the principles of effectiveness, democracy and accountability are paramount. Other negotiating groups and individual member states have also underscored these principles, which in our view can only be meaningfully upheld through periodic elections that provide all Member States with the opportunity to participate in the Council composition. We remain firmly convinced that the introduction of new permanent seats, as proposed by some, runs counter to the democratic values the Council should embody. With respect to the proposal presented by the co-chairs, it may be useful to clarify that this was introduced orally during an interactive informal session and has not been formally circulated in writing. Any proposal would benefit from reflecting the interlinkage across all 5 clusters rather than focusing exclusively on 2 of them. We value the intention of the co-chairs to direct discussions and bridge positions through this proposal, which will require further discussion in the next IGN session. In particular with reference to the veto, the expansion of the permanent category through the fixed regional seats, and its implication for accountability. On paragraph 3, we suggest replacing key parameters by guiding principles as referred to in Action 39 of the Pact for the Future. On paragraph 6, we welcome the acknowledgement that reform should prioritize enhancing the representation of underrepresented and unrepresented regions and groups. This includes the Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, in addition to the broadly recognized imperative of improving African representation. Under paragraph 7, concerning the inclusion of a review clause in a comprehensive reform of the Security Council, we suggest a more balanced reflection of the discussions. Many delegations support a review mechanism to assess whether a reformed Council is functioning more effectively and transparently in the years following the reform. However, it must be also noted that several member states oppose any approach that could serve as a vehicle for incremental or selective gains, or that could lead to a piecemeal reform. Finally, we believe that this process would be significantly strengthened by broader participation. Many Member States and the negotiating groups have yet to voice their views in the IGN. Given the importance and sensitivity of the reform agenda, and the need to ensure that any outcome enjoys the widest possible political acceptance, We encourage all Member States and the negotiating groups, particularly those who have not yet done so, to actively engage and, where possible, present their own proposals or models for reform. Under the divergence of the elements of general convergence and divergence, we align with the recognition that further steps are required before moving to text-based negotiations. However, I agree. it is important that a transition to this phase is done once convergence on all clusters of reform and broad political will are reached. We want to ensure that the conditions are in place to ensure that these needed reforms will be sustainable. On paragraph 2 of the divergence, we suggest adding, and I quote, sovereign equality among member states and accountability, and of "effectiveness." Sovereign equality is a concept mentioned in the UN Charter, but never appears in these element papers. Concerning the clusters on categories of membership, the formulation— and I quote— while there are different views on the categories of membership in a reformed Council, a significant number of delegations present in the meetings argue that the enlargement should include expansion in both the permanent and non-permanent categories, end of quote, does not accurately reflect the reality. First, as we have said before, because a significant number of Member States have not stated their views yet in the IGN, it is important to avoid overgeneralization about the state of convergence. In this regard, a distinction must be made between the views expressed —by negotiating groups and those of the wider UN membership, especially considering that some groups have overlapping compositions. Second, it is important to clearly distinguish between the nature of the permanent seats advocated by some Member States and the negotiating groups. In particular, some proposals envision permanent seats of a regional nature, such as those requested under the Common African Position. In contrast, other proposals, such as those put forward by the Group of Four, seek individual permanent seats that would represent only the respective member states themselves. The discussion of new models in the current AGN process gave even further visibility to those divergences. Third, others support the creation of new permanent seats but without veto. And finally, the co-chair's proposal of fixed regional seats represents a further perspective on the idea of expansion in the permanent category. As you can see, divergences could not be broader. The Elements paper states that a significant number of delegations argue that the enlargement should include expansion in both categories. and that new permanent members must be granted equal standing. Putting all these seats into the same nature and claim is misleading in our view, and the paper would more accurately reflect the positions of delegations if it made this distinction clearer. We believe that the Elements paper should better reflect the significant progress made by the AGN on working methods,— and on the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly. These are two clusters that are receiving growing attention from global public opinion and from which the— and for which the international community as a whole expects meaningful improvements. Distinguished Co-Chair, and I conclude, we trust that these comments will be taken into serious consideration. The revised element papers demonstrate that Tangible progress is possible, and it confirms that the IGN remains the only valid and legitimate platform for achieving Security Council reform. We thank you once again for your dedication to this process and reiterate the UFC's full commitment to a comprehensive reform that serves the interests of the entire membership. I thank you also for your patience, and I thank you for your work. Thank you. Thank you.
I thank Italy for its statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belize on behalf of the Caribbean community.

Distinguished co-chairs, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the 14 member states of the Caribbean community. At the outset, CARICOM thanks you for the presentation of the updated elements paper. Reflecting the status of discussions within the IGN on both the substantive and procedural issues related to the reform of the Security Council. CARICOM also takes this opportunity to acknowledge your exceptional stewardship of IGN and the commitment you have demonstrated to moving the needle forward. A truly reformed Security Council is one that is agile in its response to threats to international peace and security, guided by the principles of the Charter, and given the importance of the reform, CARICOM joins other member states in advocating for an injection of greater urgency in IGN, the regularization of its working methods to align them with other negotiating processes, and the revitalization of the IGN to achieve Security Council reform in the short term.

Co-chairs.

Co-chairs, CARICOM looks forward to your guidance regarding the next steps in the IGN process for this session and renews to you our full support in the execution of your important work. And I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belize for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Denmark on behalf of the Nordic countries.

Sis, chairs, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the Nordic countries, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, and my own country, Denmark. Let me begin by thanking the co-chairs for the revised Elements Paper. This serves as a fundamental document for taking these negotiations forward, and we continue to stress the importance of updating this document. While we would have hoped that this 80th session would have concluded with a consolidated model, we are grateful for your tireless efforts throughout this session. We want to thank you for the new initiatives taken during this session, including your efforts to make the discussions more focused your push for bridging divergences and for putting your own bridging proposals on the table. Cheers. The Element paper sets out that a consolidated model has emerged as an important objective of moving the IGN process forward, but also notes that mutually exclusive positions will need to be bridged before such model can be presented. While we, of course, support the notion that divergences should be bridged, we question if this is not a process that could be done through work on a consolidated model. We must recall that these negotiations have now been going on for 17 years. And when establishing this process, we gave ourselves the mandate to find a solution, and I quote, "that can garner the widest possible political acceptance by member states," end of quote. The calls for a consolidated model and the sense of urgency expressed by member states have only grown larger during this past session. And we believe that this can be better reflected in the Elements paper. Chairs, the Elements paper accurately reflects that a significant number of delegations have expressed support for an expansion in both categories. We would encourage that the groups supporting this view are reflected in the paper. While the paper reflects the support by many member states of ensuring equality in the permanent category, the paper could better reflect the concerns expressed by many delegations of the negative impact of the veto on the work and functioning of the current and the future— and enlarged Council. Cheers. We welcome that the element paper reflects a significant and growing number of member states expressing support for limitations to the scope and use of the veto, including the growing number of supporters of the ACT Code of Conduct and the French-Mexican initiative. We would encourage that the number of signatories to these initiatives be reflected in the paper. There has been broad support for a time-bound review clause as a fundamental element in any reform proposal. We believe the Elements paper could be updated to not only reflect agreement of such review clause—— to be considered, but rather that there is agreement that it should in fact be included in any reform proposal. We are also of the view that member states have not only reiterated the need to implement all provisions of the Charter, but rather the obligation to do so, which could also be updated in the Elements Paper. Cheers. As we wrap up this year's IGN session, let me reiterate the Nordic Group's steadfast support for our collective endeavor towards reform. We encourage all member states to engage constructively and in a spirit of compromise in order for a consolidated model to be developed and ultimately for text-based negotiations to be initiated. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Denmark for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines on behalf of the LCTE. L69 Group.

Co-chairs, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the L69 Group. We thank you, co-chairs, for convening this session and for transmitting the Elements Paper now before us. The group offers the following observations. The L69 Group has consistently described the Elements Paper as a record of positions. It sets out, by description, where member states converge and where they diverge.

The core purpose of the paper, in our view, is to summarize the positions of member states.

The paper records the call made by our group, together with the Benelux, the Group of Four, and the Nordic Group, to move towards the development of a consolidated model reflecting areas of convergence and divergence which could subsequently serve as the basis for text-based negotiations. We emphasize that a consolidated model which reflects both convergence and divergence must be a precursor to a text. We request that this aspect be reflected suitably in the final paper. Co-chairs, we also welcome the acknowledgment that a consolidated model would provide a concrete basis to guide the next stage of negotiations and would help translate years of deliberation into tangible outcomes. We note that the paper attaches a condition to it, that progress towards a consolidated model will first require the bridging of mutually exclusive positions. The L69 Group wishes to be clear about what a consolidated model does not do. [FOREIGN LANGUAGE] It does not select a model. It does not prejudge any contested question. Convergences enter as agreed language. Divergences enter as attributed alternatives unresolved.

It forms the basis for Member States to work with.

We acknowledge that divergences must be bridged in order to achieve progress. The L-69 Group holds that such bridging takes place through text-based negotiations. There is nothing to trade and nothing to amend until the positions are set down together, attributed in a single text. A consolidated model could provide the basis for such a text. A consolidated model must reflect every position accurately. Thank you. It must not choose. The instrument we propose is procedural. It commits the process to putting together the positions of Member States. The L69 welcomes the presentation of the African model during this session. It was a significant contribution and it gave the purpose great clarity on the common African position. A contribution of this kind is consistent with the priority the Pact attaches to redressing the historical injustice against Africa. We note that the manner in which the paper has reflected convergences and divergences warrants a review. Please allow us to elaborate. First, the fact that a majority supports expansion in the permanent category has not been taken into account. It has been reflected as a significant number. Second, as we conveyed in the previous IGN meetings, the fixed regional seats proposal is not aligned with the majority view to have an expansion in both categories. It has also been mentioned that the member states would serve in their national capacities as opposed to representatives of their respective region.

Therefore, the proposal is not in tune with the principle of regional representation either.

Third, IGN must be a member-state-driven process, as outlined in the UNGA Decision 62/557. Advancement of IGN discussions must, therefore, be based on this fundamental principle. Fourth, the definition of permanent seats is clear. The UN Charter is unambiguous in this regard. Finally, limiting the reform only to expansion of the non-permanent category does not lead to real reforms. Co-chairs, the positions of member states are known. They need to be reflected suitably in this paper.

The question now before the membership is whether they are prepared to set out those positions down in a single negotiable text.

Our group therefore proposes that the outcome of the coming cycle be the commencement of a consolidated model capturing convergences and divergences, attributed and complete. The L69 group is ready to begin that work and looks forward to engaging in that process. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines for his statement, and I now give the I now hand over to the distinguished representative of France.

Madame et Monsieur les Co-présidents, distinguished co-chairs, thank you for convening this sixth debate and for your commitment. The elements paper distributed after the five thematic debates takes the form of an update on elements of convergence and divergence shared in 2025. This revised version ought to contribute to giving new momentum to these negotiations and laying the groundwork for a future consolidated model. Distinguished co-chairs, this past year has confirmed that the call for Security Council reform has never been so broadly supported. As recalled by Secretary General, and I quote, "Our world has changed but not our institutions." We cannot effectively address the problems we're facing as they are if our institutions don't reflect the world as it is. This reality is especially true for the Security Council. To maintain its legitimacy, its authority, and its effectiveness, the Security Council must better reflect modern geopolitical realities as well as the diversity of UN member states. The Pact for the Future was a historic milestone. For the first time in decades, member states agreed on common parameters for reform, recognized the urgency of making progress. The work of this session demonstrated this trend is continuing. On the elements paper, we have 3 comments. First of all, the commitment of France toward an ambitious Security Council reform, as you know, is longstanding, clear, and unwavering. France therefore welcomes the increased convergence on several essential points: the need for a more representative council that meets the legitimate expectations of Africa and other underrepresented regions; And we welcome the consolidated paper of Africa, by the way, as well as the growing support for limiting veto usage. Secondly, despite this progress, key differences remain. The question of membership categories and the veto continue to be the subject of the main disagreements. France believes that credible reform must include an expansion of the Council in its two membership categories, permanent and non-permanent. We continue to support the creation of 2 new permanent seats for Africa in accordance with the goal of rectifying the historic injustice done to this continent. We also reaffirm our support for according permanent seats to Germany, Brazil, India, and Japan as part of a comprehensive reform. In addition, France remains in favor of an expanded council including 25 members. Thank you. Reconciling representation and effectiveness. Thirdly, the work of this session showed that a growing number of states wish to move toward a consolidated model. We have noted the efforts taken this year to identify ways of reconciling the different positions. Discussions on potential models demonstrate a shared desire to overcome traditional divisions and to reconcile the positions of member states. Thank you. Reform must now move forward based on a draft resolution that translates elements of convergence into concrete positions. The time has come to move from inventing new positions toward building compromise. Distinguished co-chairs, in closing, I'd like to underscore the role of governing the veto in the elements of convergence. We are pleased with the growing support for initiatives that aim to limit the use of the veto, especially when it comes to mass atrocities. In this regard, France renews its call for all states that have not yet done so to join the French-Mexican initiative on the voluntary suspension of veto use in the event of genocide, crimes against humanity, or crimes— massive war crimes. 118 states have already supported this initiative, which is a response to the calls of the international community and is an immediate way of strengthening responsibility of the Council with regard to the most serious crimes. In a context marked by increasing numbers of crises and mass violations of international humanitarian law, we call on all member states to join the collective effort. Lastly, France will continue its commitment for ambitious balanced and broadly supported reform. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of France for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt.

Thank you, co-chairs. At the outset, my delegation aligns with the statements that will be delivered later today by Sierra Leone on behalf of the African Group and Bahrain on behalf of the Arab Group. Co-chairs, we took note of your letter dated 10th June 2026 and the attached revised elements paper on convergences and divergences in the IGN process for this session. We acknowledge your efforts in this regard. We welcome the submission of this important document and would like to make the following remarks regarding its nature. First, Egypt considers this document to be exclusively reflective of the views of the IGN co-chairs for what they deem as areas of convergences and divergences during the IGN at the 80th session of the General Assembly. This document remains neither exhaustive nor conclusive, nor is it a final representation of the views of member states Member States and political groups substantively or procedurally. Second, Egypt reiterates that nothing in this revised elements paper shall be construed as binding to Member States and political groups, nor shall it be considered as a basis for any text-based negotiation on the question of the reform of the Security Council. Co-chairs, allow me to also make the following remarks on the substance of the Elements Paper. First, Egypt welcomes updating the Elements Paper to reflect the introduction and subsequent discussion on the African Model for Reform. We also welcome the references in the overall convergences on the necessity of addressing the historical injustice against Africa as a priority and that Africa should be treated as a special case. The African Model for Reform is the embodiment of this wide agreement. Thank you.— in the IGN. Based on the common African position as outlined in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirt Declaration, the African model envisages two permanent African seats with the veto and two additional non-permanent African seats. In our view, this is the one and only path towards addressing the historical injustice that has befallen the African continent since the inception of this organization. Second, we took note of the inclusion in the Elements Paper of the fixed regional seats proposal, as set forth by the co-chairs in the first informal discussion on January 21, 2026. This would be the very first time this proposal is put on paper by the co-chairs, and while we acknowledge the framing of this proposal in the Elements Paper as belonging to the co-chairs, we believe the language in the introduction should be strengthened to further reflect this fact. We believe that including the fixed seats proposal in the revised Elements Paper will give it a life of its own in perpetuity, as it will continue to feature in successive iterations of the Elements Paper. That's why it is crucially important that the paper leaves no room for interpretation about the nature of this proposal being exclusively put forward on the responsibility solely of the co-chairs. Third, we have and will continue to engage constructively in the discussions on the various reform models presented by groups and member states, as well as on other proposals. Nevertheless, we note that in paragraph 1 under elements of general divergences, a reference is made to a consolidated model as being the stepping stone towards text-based negotiations in the view of some groups. While we support the mandate given to the co-chairs in the Pact of the Future to develop a consolidated model, we don't believe that making a reference to this model as being the precursor to text-based negotiations is factually accurate, even when put under divergences and even in the context of the views of specific groups and countries. The pact of the future is clear. The envisaged consolidated model is only one way of progressing discussions in the IGN. It is not the only way. The pact also does not establish any link between the consolidated model and text-based negotiations. Assuming that such model would be the basis for negotiations is simply prejudging the contents of this model, before it has even been drafted. We continue to believe that no text-based negotiations can commence before preliminary agreement on the fundamental aspects of reform. This agreement is not here yet, as acknowledged in the elements paper itself. Egypt is of the view that this link between the consolidated model and text-based negotiations should be removed from the paper. Lastly, paragraph 8 in the Elements of General Convergences makes a claim that, and I quote, "Several delegations mentioned the full and consistent application of Article 27(3) 27(3) as a practical avenue to constrain the use of the veto within the current framework. While we acknowledge the value of the application of Article 27(3) 27(3) and how it can curb the use of the veto, we don't subscribe to the notion that it is a substitute for veto reform." and certainly not under convergences. Decision 62557 is clear on the veto being one of the key pillars of reform. Discussions on the application of Article 27(3) 27(3) are thus not part of this IGM process and cannot by any means feature under convergences in the Elements Paper. Co-chairs, turning to the way forward as we end the session's deliberations, We look forward to a smooth rollover process of the IGN to the coming session of the General Assembly. We believe that the rollover decision should be adopted as soon as possible, before the end of this month or mostly early next month. Unnecessary delays should be avoided at all costs. We remain committed to the negotiations. We thank you, co-chairs, for your efforts throughout this session. We look forward to receiving the revised— revised elements paper and we look forward to continue working with you and everyone else in the 81st session. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt for his statement and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain.

Muchas gracias. Thank you very much, Madam Co-Chair. Spain is a part of the Uniting for Consensus Group, supports and aligns itself with the statement delivered by Italy. And I will now make some additional remarks in my national capacity. We would like to begin by saying that we're very grateful for the circulation of the co-chair's paper on the revised elements of convergence and divergence. And we see a set of important issues reflected there, including the increasingly widespread support to limit the use and scope of the veto to Resolution 76/262 on the veto initiative, as well as the need to apply all articles of the UN Charter, including Article 27(3). 27(3). Secondly, I would like to highlight the divergences. It is noted that the divergences The divergences on the issue of the veto are mainly driven by concerns relating to equality between permanent members. Therefore, in our view, the use of the veto goes much further than what is reflected in— this divergence, this point. I'd also like to refer to something that other delegations have already touched on relating to the Pact for the Future. Thank you, Chair. Distinguished co-chairs, the Arab Group welcomes the reaffirmation in the Elements Paper of the dire need to reform the Security Council and that the IGN remains the sole inclusive and legitimate member states-led framework to address this issue. We agree that the goal of the reform is to reach a more representative, inclusive, transparent, effective, and accountable Council so as to enhance its legitimacy and its ability to shoulder its responsibilities in the maintenance of international peace and security. The deliberations during the session have demonstrated the persistence of fundamental differences amongst member states on a number of core issues. Namely the categories of memberships, the veto, and regional representation. Any durable progress requires that we address in a balanced and comprehensive manner such issues by avoiding piecemeal or selective approaches. Distinguished co-chairs, on the consolidated model, the Arab Group underlines That any such model must be underpinned by genuine convergences reached amongst member states. It must reflect in a balanced manner all models and proposals provided by member states and negotiating groups. The development of a consolidated model should not precede nor supplant a consensus on core principles but must rather be a natural product of such consensus. Interventions of member states and negotiating groups have revealed divergences in positions on the reform model as well as the way forward for the IGN, in particular regarding proposals on text-based negotiations.
Thank you.

Thus, any progress requires careful deliberation and flexibility. Imposing any non-consensual steps amongst member states will undermine the unity of the membership and erode the credibility of the IGN. The Arab group underlines the need to preserve the unity amongst member states Member states. Flexibility must be demonstrated to reach consensus. We must also avoid artificial timeframes as well as contentious steps, as well as the development of a consolidated model before consensus is reached amongst member states and negotiating groups on core principles for reform, which could undermine efforts for reform in general. The Arab Group reiterates that the 5 clusters provided for in GA Decision 62/557 are closely interlinked. They cannot be addressed separately. Therefore, any future— a future model must address in a balanced manner the categories of membership, regional representation, the veto,— the size and methods of work of the Council and its relationship with the GA. Distinguished co-chairs, we reiterate that Arab representation within the Council remains one of its most fundamental gaps in its composition. Despite the political and demographic weight of the Arab Group, as well as its vital relevance to the work of the Security Council, The Arab group still lacks permanent representation within the council. Any genuine and credible reform, therefore, must address this imbalance by ensuring a permanent Arab representation in any future reform formula. Any expansion in the permanent category must be underpinned by full equality in rights and privileges. If the veto remains, the principle of equality precludes the establishment of permanent categories that are not granted the same rights and prerogatives. Distinguished co-chairs, the Arab Group commits to constructively and responsibly engaging in the process. We will work with all partners to reach an inclusive and balanced reform with the widest political acceptance amongst member states one that reflects contemporary international realities and promote the efficiency and credibility of the Council.

The distinguished representative of Kenya.

Co-chairs, Kenya recognizes the challenge of faithfully capturing the breadth and complexity of views expressed throughout this IGN cycle and appreciates the considerable effort invested in preparing the revised Elements Paper and in steering the process with transparency and balance. We align ourselves with the statement delivered by Equatorial Guinea on behalf of the African Group and offer the following reflections in our national capacity.
Thank you.

In the introductory assessment of the current cycle, the paper underscores that despite widespread support for reform, the membership has yet to reach a common understanding on the architecture of a reformed Council. It also records broad agreement that reform must deliver a Council that's more representative effective, transparent, and accountable, consistent with the pact for the future. Yet significant divergences persist, particularly in categories of membership, regional representation, and the question of the veto, which continues to shape the pace and direction of our negotiations. Kenya encourages adoption of a results-oriented approach, that enables the membership to narrow gaps where divergences persist. Co-chairs, the veto remains one of the most divisive issues in the IGF process, with member states holding differing views on its retention, its reform, its limitation, or its extension. Kenya supports efforts to limit the use of the veto including through full and consistent application of Article 27(3), 27(3), while reaffirming that equitable treatment of all permanent members is essential to a credible reform outcome. Africa's representation and the historical injustice is at the heart of this debate. The paper notes the growing recognition of Africa's legitimate aspiration to play its rightful role. Kenya welcomes this acknowledgement in paragraph 6 of the Convergences section. Africa's exclusion remains a fundamental gap in the Council's representativeness, and any credible reform outcome must meaningfully redress this injustice in line with the Pact for the Future, the principles of sovereign equality, and equitable geographical representation. Future negotiations should therefore focus on practical modalities that enhance Africa's presence and decision-making role while preserving Africa's right to determine its own representatives and ensuring the widest possible political acceptance. We also note the increasing emphasis by member states on accountability, and review mechanisms as essential to a more legitimate and effective Council. This aligns with concerns reflected across the paper regarding decision-making processes, equity, and the need for more systematic engagement with the wider UN membership. While there's general support for refining working methods, divergence remains on the extent and modalities of such reform, particularly how to balance efficiency with inclusivity, limiting coherence across the reform clusters. Co-chairs, Kenya supports a pragmatic and inclusive approach that builds on emerging convergences, including improving reporting practices, strengthening General Assembly engagement, and exploring flexible, mutually agreed periodic review frameworks to ensure that reform remains adaptable to future realities. In this regard, we underline the importance of maintaining clarity regarding the status of the Elements Paper. Its value lies in helping the membership identify areas of progress, remaining differences, and potential pathways towards convergence as envisaged in paragraphs 13 and 17. As we move into the next phase of negotiations, Kenya encourages that four mutually reinforcing principles guide our collective efforts, and these are: One, that the reform addresses historical inequities, including the underrepresentation of Africa. Two, that the reform examines the use of the veto to identify possible areas of agreement. Three, that the reform strengthens the legitimacy, effectiveness, and accountability of the Council. And four, that the reform commands the widest possible political acceptance among member states, consistent with Decision 62. /557. Kenya remains committed to engaging constructively with all member states in pursuit of a reformed Security Council that reflects today's realities and is equipped to meet tomorrow's challenges. I thank you.

However, the working principle in the Elements Paper regarding convergences and divergences are different and ambiguous and subjective understanding and views of the co-chairs. Second, UNGA Decision 62/557 clearly stipulates that the purpose behind the IGN is to garner a solution with the widest possible political acceptance based on proposals by member states. This foundational document of the IGN does not mention about—
Thank you.

Or allude to bridging proposals. It has also been the firm established practice in the UN for the co-chairs or co-facs to propose bridging proposals after floating a text as part of text-based negotiations and not before. It would also be contextual to highlight that the Elements Paper treats a reform of the Security Council as a member states-driven process.
