It further adds that member states elected to such seats would serve in their national capacity and not formally represent their respective regions. These present three inherent issues.
Thank you.

One, the proposal in no way expands a permanent category. Two, the concept of regionality would not be served if the concerned member states act in their national capacities. And three, it weakens the case of SIDS, a cross-regional group which India has been consistently supportive of. Further, this whole proposal is akin to granting a veto to the E10, bereft of convoluted arguments of permanency. This proposal confuses veto power with permanency. Fourth, the elements paper proposes further discussion and clarification on the concept of permanency. The UN Charter is very clear on this question and there is no room for ambiguity. Article 23 clearly categorizes the UNSC members into two: permanent and non-permanent. Therefore, the definition of a permanent seat needs no further elaboration of classification as a divergence. Groups and member states, including the African Group, the G4, and L69, treat a permanent member serving or future strictly in accordance with the provisions of the Charter. Further, on convergences under regional representation, there is no mention of the broad support for improving the representation of African group in the UN Security Council. The IGN meeting that focused on presentation of the African model had made the supportive views of all key stakeholders known. Fifth, as also highlighted in the past, support of a majority for expansion in the permanent category has been reduced to— a significant number of delegations in the elements paper. Despite the categorical position of a majority of member states in favor of expanding the permanent category, as reflected either in the national statements delivered at the IGN or through association with groups such as L69, G4, CARICOM, etc., this has not been depicted accurately. Sixth, reflecting expansion of the category of two-year term non-permanent category as a convergence, portrays only a part of the picture. Groups and member states add qualifiers and attach other interlinked parameters as they endorse expansion in the non-permanent category. UNSC reform would be grossly inadequate, bordering on failure, if expansion is limited only to the non-permanent category, as it would fundamentally not change the decision-making power structure of the P5. Groups and member states have waited this long for real and meaningful reforms. Seventh, a nothing-is-agreed-until-everything-is-agreed approach must not become a tool to block progress. Status quoists have tried to use this argument in their favor and thereby entrench the existing inequities in the Security Council. Eighth, the General Assembly is a truly democratic principal organ of the UN. However, the Security Council is fundamentally different by its very design. By advocating expansion of the permanent category, India's consistent effort has been to bring in a greater sense of balance and equity in the Security Council and change the decision-making parameters of the P5 while being mindful that the principle of sovereign equality of states would not be applicable in its entirety, unlike the UNGA, due to such foundational DNA enshrined in the Charter. Finally, IGN cannot be fundamentally different from other UN processes wherein negotiations are held on the basis of a text. —groups and member states express their views on the text under consideration. Therefore, we urge the co-chairs to take the lead on formulating a text with clearly defined milestones and timelines so that groups and member states could engage in a purposeful and outcome-oriented manner, and thereafter consider, if necessary and as appropriate, any bridging proposal. In closing, it is India's sincere hope that the co-chairs would suitably take into account our views and amend the elements paper suitably in order to make it more objective. India would also like to reiterate that we will continue to support all earnest efforts by the co-chairs and other groups and member states towards achieving real reforms of the UN Security Council. Shukran Jazilan.

I thank the representative of India.

I give the floor now to the representative of Argentina.

Thank you very much, Mr. Co-chair. Allow me to begin by thanking both co-facilitators for their efforts this session and for the preparation of the revised paper on elements of convergence and diversion. Argentina is grateful for the compilation of the member states' positions and the positions of groups of interests over the current current session. My delegation also aligns itself with the statement delivered by Italy on behalf of Uniting for Consensus, and we'd like to add the following in our national capacity. Firstly, Argentina welcomes the fact that the document reflects areas of convergence reached up to date, as well as those areas where substantive differences persist among member states. This is essential to preserve the inclusive and transparent nature of the process. My delegation notes that the document includes new references to the potential development of a consolidated model. In this regard, Argentina believes that any discussion on future stages of the process should be grounded in the prior forging of genuine convergences among member states, particularly with regard to membership categories and the issue of the veto— areas where Fundamental differences remain. We also take note of the proposal relating to the so-called fixed regional seats. In my delegation's view, this proposal would call for greater details for member states, particularly on issues related to accountability, the periodic review mechanisms, regional selection procedures, and the potential relationship with the prerogatives currently associated with permanent members. Thank you. Argentina particularly welcomes the fact that the document reflects that many member states continue to consider that solely the periodic elections by the General Assembly can fully guarantee accountability and the democratic legitimacy of the Security Council's composition. In my delegation's view, this principle remains one of the central elements of this reform process. Furthermore, Argentina understands that to move towards greater convergence, it's essential to continue encouraging member states and groups of states to present models. Recent experiences, including the African group, have contributed to enriching the debate and clarifying positions on fundamental issues. On the references to the Pact for the Future, Argentina would like to recall that the IGN stems from and its mandate is contained in Decision 62557. Chair. General Assembly. This remains the agreed framework for this process. In representativeness, Argentina believes it's necessary to continue paying particular attention to historically underrepresented regions in the Security Council. In this context, Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean, and Asia Pacific continue to face representation deficits that must be addressed. To conclude, Argentina reaffirms its commitment to a member-state-driven reform process that is inclusive, transparent, and based on the quest for the broadest possible consensus. The Argentina— the IGN should continue to make gradual but sustained progress, avoiding approaches that would artificially speed up discussions before there being sufficient convergences. My delegation believes that any potential progress towards new stages of the process should, in a balanced manner, reflect the positions expressed by all member states and interest groups, preserving the principle that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Argentina.
And I give the floor to the Russian Federation.

Distinguished co-coordinators, we thank you for convening today's meeting and preparing the latest draft document on elements of divergence and convergence positions of member states on Security Council reform. We highly value your intensive efforts throughout this 80th session. The obvious outcome of the session, as he rightly noted in the document, is the persistence of exclusive positions on key reform parameters, including with regard to veto rights and membership categories. At the same time, we believe that even on these issues of In principle, there has been progress. In particular, when discussing veto rights, we regularly hear from the vast majority of delegations, including the major opponents of this mechanism, that the abolition of the veto would be an unrealistic goal. And that means that all that is possible is individual voluntary commitments not to use the veto. We believe that this could be reflected— that is, this predominant opinion could be reflected in the elements paper. In addition, we believe that the draft paper's call to work on a consolidated model is a goal that requires a sensitive and progressive approach. As noted in the Pact for the Future, this concept ought to be based not only on the models presented but also on elements of convergence on all 5 thematic clusters. As we have repeatedly noted during this session, none of the models presented, unfortunately, is sufficiently promising to serve as the basis for package decision. Under these conditions, work to reconcile differences on the 5 thematic clusters must continue.
Thank you.

Thank you, distinguished co-chairs. We have 3 additional comments to the text with regard to principle. The first concerns the section on regional representation that is on page 15, where an additional assertion now states that in addition to Asia, Africa, and Latin America, another underrepresented region is Eastern Europe. This assertion is highly controversial. It contradicts the key goal of the reform, which is to increase representation for developing countries in the composition of the Council. We fundamentally disagree that the Council ought to be expanded to include developed countries from this region. The majority of these states also— adhere to the bloc approaches of NATO and the EU and cannot contribute constructively to the work of the Council. Our second comment concerns the mention of the Pact for the Future itself in the introduction to the document, where it states that the pact is the product of broad consensus. I'd like to recall that Russia distanced itself from consensus at the adoption of this document for a number of reasons. Thank you. Controversial language was forced through during the drafting of this document, and as a result, it is not the product of a real agreement between member states, and therefore, it disappointed many countries, including Russia. We call on you, distinguished co-coordinators, to correct the paper accordingly. Thirdly, we agree with many delegations that it is not is not currently helpful to mention in the Elements Paper the proposal on the permanent regional seat. We appreciate your efforts to seek compromise on the reform, but we believe it is not right that the paper speaks about a concept that up until now has not been presented or supported by a member of the IGN. In addition, the draft did not reflect, unfortunately, our proposal on introducing the concept of overrepresented and sufficiently represented regional groups. It's obvious to us that the first category, the overrepresented group, ought to include the Western Europe and Others group. We hold that this kind of reference would allow us to narrow the scope of the reform. We hope that This proposal will continue to be discussed at the next session. In closing, I'd like to once again thank you for your conscientious leadership of the IGN during this session and to express our hope for continued progressive work to find new compromises on Security Council reform. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative representative of Poland.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair. At the outset, Poland would like to express its sincere appreciation to the Co-Chairs for convening this meeting and for the preparation of the revised Co-Chairs' Elements Paper. We have been actively engaged in the discussions within the IGFN and we welcome the fact that our perspective as a country not affiliated with any negotiating group and a member of Eastern European Group underrepresented in the United Nations Security Council is reflected in the substance of the document. We also would like to thank the co-chairs for their leadership and their pragmatic, progress-oriented approach. We appreciate the introduction of the bridging proposal on fixed regional seats. Poland stands ready to engage constructively in discussions on initiatives that could help build the broadest possible consensus among the member states. We further comment the inclusion of convergence point number 8 concerning the full and consistent application of Article 27, paragraph 3 of the Charter. We see that this is a practical and realistic avenue to constrain the use of the veto within the existing legal framework. While comprehensive reform of the Security Council requiring Charter amendment remains a complex and long-term endeavor, the Charter itself already provides tools that could improve the Council's functioning. These tools should be fully utilized, including in the spirit of the commitments we have collectively undertaken in the Pact of the Future. In this context, Poland also supports the notion that incremental changes to the working methods and functioning of the Council, within its current structure and without requiring amendments to the Charter, can enhance its efficiency, effectiveness inclusiveness, and transparency. Mr. Co-Chair, at the same time, as noted in the divergence number 2, addressing the issue of the veto remains crucial. Allow me to offer a simple analogy: expanding the Council without tackling the problem of the veto is like adding more carriages to the train that is struggling to leave the station. While adding carriages is justified and necessary, it will not bring us closer to our destination, namely the maintenance of international peace and security if the engine itself is not functioning properly. Unless we address the underlying mechanisms, the system will remain impaired. Poland remains committed to working with the IGF in a constructive and pragmatic manner to advance this important process in the future.

And I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland for his statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

[SPEAKING CHINESE] Co-chairs, under your leadership, this session of the IGN has carried out comprehensive discussions on the five clusters, the African reform model, and fixed regional seats, among others. This has enabled better understanding of each other's positions and helped build consensus and narrow differences, fully demonstrating the value of the IGN and showing good progress. China positively commends all your efforts. On the draft revised co-chairs' elements paper, China would like to emphasize the following 3 points. First, the nature of the co-chairs' paper is a personal summary prepared by the co-chairs. Based on their own observations and understanding of the discussions among member states, the co-chairs summarized and synthesized the current IGN session and presented the revised co-chairs' paper. This is standard practice in intergovernmental negotiations and can serve as useful reference for the next session, but it does not constitute the basis of a text for negotiations. Second, The co-chairs' paper must objectively reflect the views and positions of all parties, as well as the current status of the IGM. Given the discussions held during this IGM session, member states remain deeply divided on the 5 clusters. However, the co-chairs' paper fails to accurately capture this. On categories of membership, member states have put forward a variety of ideas At present, consensus has been reached only on expanding the non-permanent category, while other proposals require further deliberation. At the same time, an increasing number of countries are open to the idea of creating regional and rotating seats. China believes that it is necessary to reflect these ideas and views objectively and equitably in the co-chair's paper. On regional representation and seat allocation, The general consensus among all parties is that the only correct direction for reform is to enhance the representation of developing countries. Continuing to add seats for Western developed countries does not align with the expectations of all parties. On permanency and the veto power, the co-chairs' paper has recognized divergences among member states on these matters, Therefore, sensitive issues such as restricting the veto power touch upon the very foundation of the UN's decision-making mechanisms and therefore must be handled with caution to avoid jumping to any conclusions. Third, the principle of consensus among member states must be upheld. It is important to encourage member states to engage in in-depth discussions based on reform proposals submitted by various parties and further building consensus on the five clusters. Formulating a consolidated model in a hasty manner requiring imposing an artificial timetable for reform or even threatening to start everything from scratch at the General Assembly runs counter to General Assembly Resolution 62/557 and the spirit of the Pact for the Future. Such an approach would exacerbate division and confrontation among member states and undermine the healthy momentum of Council reform. China opposes this approach and hopes that the broad membership will stay vigilant. Co-chairs, this IGF session is nearing the completion of its mandated tasks. China supports the co-chairs starting the rollover as scheduled and to maintain the overall reform process and the unity among member states, We would like to see the co-chairs refine the draft co-chairs paper in a fair and transparent manner, thus laying the foundation for the successful and timely conclusion of this IGN session. And putting in the groundwork for the next session of the IGN, China will work with all parties to uphold the role of IGN as the main channel and continue discussions to build consensus on the 5 clusters at the next session of the GA so as to jointly advance the Council reform in a direction that serves the common interests of member states and the long-term development of the UN. China will continue to support the efforts of the co-chairs going forward. Thank you, co-chairs.
I thank the distinguished representative of China for his statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa.

Thank you, Co-Chair. South Africa aligns with the statements delivered on behalf of the Africa Group and the L69. Co-Chairs, it's unacceptable that the Security Council continues to disproportionately serve the interests of a small number of permanent members. South Africa is therefore appreciative of the revised Elements Paper as a reflection of the progress that has been made through the intergovernmental negotiations on Security Council reform. The revised Elements Paper could be an effort towards negotiations. However, it would benefit from further strengthening to better reflect discussions within the IGN. Generally— The revised Elements Paper could further be improved by attributing of positions from each of the groups or individual delegations on issues related to the different clusters. We welcome references to the commitments made by the Heads of State and Government in the Pact for the Future. In our view, Action 41A was instructive in that the consolidated model should be based on the convergences of the 5 clusters. We therefore do not understand this to mean that to have a consolidated model requires us to first bridge mutually exclusive positions, particularly on the question of the veto and categories of membership, as indicated in the Elements Paper. The identification of areas of convergence in the Elements Paper could serve as a basis for the consolidated model. We welcome the recognition of growing support for Africa's representation on the Security Security Council in order to redress the historical injustices against Africa and to advance its treatment as a special case. We also acknowledge that there is increasing convergence on the need for representation of underrepresented and unrepresented regions, including Asia-Pacific as well as Latin America and the Caribbean, which many groups and member states have supported.
Thank you.

Co-chairs, we do note, however, that there is yet to be agreement on the representation of other regions and cross-regional groups. Further discussions are required on this matter, taking into consideration the views expressed by some groups and member states that a reformed Security Council should have equitable regional representation and should not result in the overrepresentation of some regions. The revised Elements Paper should reflect this. Regarding the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly, we propose including in the Elements Paper an updated reference to the latest General Assembly resolution on the revitalization of the work of the General Assembly, namely Resolution 79/327 of 5 September 2025. Thank you. Lastly, the revised Elements Paper should, in our view, also recognize the broad support for text-based negotiations as advocated by multiple groups and not limit the discussions on this matter to divergences. South Africa reiterates that the urgent need to advance such negotiations, which would facilitate engagement on differing perspectives, and proposed models and thereby support progress towards consensus on the Security Council reform should be concluded. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa for his statement and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Germany.

Thank you, distinguished co-chairs. Germany aligns itself fully with the statement that has been delivered by Japan this morning on behalf of the Group of Four. I would like to make 4 brief points in my national capacity. First and foremost, we unfortunately continue to believe that the Elements Paper does not adequately reflect the current state of discussion. In our view, the main reason is that positions are presented without attribution. As a result, the paper does not show how many member states actually stand behind a respective— position, and this matters gravely. Positions that enjoy the support for more— of more than half of the membership, and for example, just take the expansion in both categories, which clearly is represented by more than half, are not listed as such and they're not listed as a convergence. Second, we disagree with the statement that progress towards a consolidated model will first require bridging mutually exclusive positions, and here I echo what my colleague from South Africa said. Our clear preference would be to develop an open consolidated model that reflects the diverging positions. These divergences should then be dealt with during the next phase, which for us clearly is text-based negotiations. Third, we are not persuaded by the newly introduced discussion on what permanency is supposed to mean. In our view, this debate risks becoming a distraction from the real issue. If delegations call for expansion in the permanent category, we should take that member state positions seriously and we should take them at face value. The task before us is not to reinterpret clearly expressed positions but to register them faithfully and work from there. Fourth and finally, on the idea of fixed regional seats, We appreciate the intention to search for bridging proposals. We see value in efforts to identify common ground. This being said, we do not see how this particular idea bridges the underlying differences. A large majority of member states— and here I repeat myself— supports the addition of new permanent members. The majority cannot reasonably feel reflected in a model based on seats that are not permanent or not as permanent as the existing P5. For that reason, we believe this proposal catches neither the political reality nor the viewpoints of the membership. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany for her statement and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Vietnam.

Co-chairs, I thank you for convening this meeting and for the circulation of the revised co-chairs' Elements Paper. My delegation commends the co-chairs for your dedicated efforts and for conducting the process in a transparent, inclusive, and member-state-driven process.
Emmanuel.

Vietnam welcomes the revised Elements Paper and recognizes its value to advancing the reform. By systematically identifying areas of convergence and divergence across the 5 clusters, The paper has enhanced transparency, clarity, and accessibility of the IGN process. We are particularly encouraged to see that areas of both agreement and differences are being explored at greater depth and detail. We also appreciate the approach adopted by the co-chairs this year of dedicating specific meetings to individual clusters and reform models. These focused discussions have helped clarify positions, deepen our understanding of the various proposals before us, and identify possible avenues for bridging differences. The structured exchange on reform models submitted during this and previous sessions have been particularly useful in this regard. Co-chairs, at a time when the international communities face increasingly complex and evolving challenges. Meaningful Security Council reform is essential to enhancing the Council's credibility, legitimacy, and effectiveness in discharging its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. Vietnam therefore continues to support expansion in both the permanent and non-permanent categories of membership in accordance with the principle of equitable geographical representation. Particular attention should be given to addressing the longstanding underrepresentation of the Africa and Asia-Pacific regions, whose memberships and contributions to the UN have not been adequately reflected in the current composition of the Council. We underscore the interlinkages between the five clusters and reaffirm the principles that have guided the IJN process. At the same time, Madagascar would be supportive— building further on areas where broad convergence has already emerged. Reform of the Council working methods is one such area where tangible progress could contribute to enhancing the Council's transparency, accountability, and effectiveness. Exploring these areas of convergence in a more concrete and detailed manner could help gradually narrow differences, strengthen mutual understanding, and contribute to identifying practical pathways toward reform outcomes capable of commanding the widest possible political acceptance. Finally, we would be interested in hearing the co-chairs' reflections on the way forward, including how the work undertaken during these sessions may help advance discussion in the next session of the G8. Please be assured of Vietnam's full and steadfast support to you, co-chairs, and for the pursuit of meaningful progress on Security Council reform. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Vietnam for her statement, and I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you, co-chairs. Thank you very much, as ever, for convening us today and for sharing the draft of the elements paper. The United Kingdom values the sessions and discussions that we have held during this year's IGN. Which have enabled detailed exchanges across all 5 clusters, including on categories of membership, the veto, regional representation, and working methods. We have also benefited from engagement with specific models and ideas, including the presentation of the African model. We reiterate our firm support for the IGN as the member-state-led forum through which progress on Security Council reform should be pursued. Thank you. We continue to call for a Council that is more representative of the world today and better able to respond to contemporary challenges. We agree that much of what is included in the Elements Paper reflects the breadth of our discussions this year, but would like to suggest further consideration of a few points. Firstly, we believe it remains important to ensure clarity on the IGN's mandate.

Mandate.

As agreed in the Pact for the Future, the focus of this process should be on advancing agreement on reform parameters, including through identifying areas of convergence and moving towards a consolidated model. We welcome the already strong collaboration between the Security Council and the General Assembly, and in relation to this cluster, we would encourage a continued focus on those elements most relevant to Security Council reform. We underline the importance of referring to existing practice and ensuring alignment with established frameworks, including Note 507. We would also recommend referencing the efforts the Security Council has already undertaken to improve the process around annual reports and the existing engagement of member states with the work of the Council. To this end, we suggest that it is worthwhile to focus on improving the 'engagement' of the General Assembly with the work of the Security Council and its subsidiary organs, rather than 'participation', as it is put in 2.2.4 in the Elements Paper, which confuses the role of the GA as a whole and the vital role of non-permanent members. We continue to attach high importance to the full and active participation of non-permanent members in in the Council's work, including through the chairing of subsidiary bodies and penholder roles. More broadly on working methods, discussions this year have underlined the importance of ensuring that an enlarged Council remains effective and able to act. The UK has consistently emphasized that any expansion must enhance both the representativeness and the functionality of the Council. We agree that consideration of working methods in the context of enlargement will be essential, while recalling that working methods remain primarily a matter for the Council itself. Turning to the question of the veto. Discussions this year have demonstrated continued interest across the membership in improving transparency and accountability in its use. The UK remains— Sorry, one second. The UK maintains that the veto should be exercised responsibly. To this end, we were proud to co-sponsor the veto initiative that now enables the General Assembly to scrutinize the use of the veto. Finally, on regional representation. This year, the IGN sessions included a substantive discussion of the African model. We note the work undertaken by the African Union Committee of Ten in developing and presenting this proposal. As you know, the UK has long supported permanent African representation as part of a more representative Council. Further discussion will prove helpful in identifying areas of broad convergence before elements of any specific model can be reflected as agreed parameters. To close, thank you once again, co-chairs, for convening today's discussion and for your efforts in advancing this important process. Thank you. We look forward to continued engagement and constructive discussions that move us towards text-based negotiations. The UK remains a committed supporter of Security Council reform, including expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories, and of the IGN as the forum in which to build consensus and make meaningful progress. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Namibia.

Thank you, co-chairs. Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I thank you, co-chairs, for convening this meeting and appreciate your leadership in this process. Namibia aligns itself with the statement delivered by Equatorial Guinea on behalf of the African Group, and we have the honor to make additional remarks in our national capacity. Namibia remains committed to the reform of the Security Council through the IGN process and supports the co-chair's strong emphasis in the revised Elements Paper and the PEC for the Future, which created the the necessary momentum for the IGN process. The consolidated model, as called for in Action 40 of the Pact, provided a clear objective for the IGN moving forward. The consolidated model, to be informed by the various models presented, should provide a concrete basis to guide the next stage of negotiations towards tangible outcomes. Thank you. Moving from the theoretical discussions to practical and tangible engagements. There is a need for a more balanced, legitimate, and effective multilateral system through the meaningful, comprehensive, and urgent reform of the Security Council, especially for the continent that has been historically and unjustly left out. The commitment to treat Africa as a special case and priority within the IGN process must be upheld. Our demand is just, our position is clear, and our resolve is unwavering. The reform of the Security Council is indispensable to building a United Nations that is truly representative, responsive, and capable of effectively addressing the complex and interrelated challenges of our time. We therefore call for all the member states to embrace the clear and results-oriented roadmap provided in the Pact, as reiterated by the co-chairs in the revised Elements Paper, in order to translate the enhanced political momentum created towards concrete text-based negotiations in the IGN process. I thank you, co-chairs.
I thank the distinguished representative of Namibia for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Romania.

Thank you, esteemed co-chairs. We welcome the Elements Paper as a stocktake of options, competing ideas, but also aspects of The 80th anniversary of the UN offers a symbolic moment for reflection, reform, and readaptation to the current international challenges, to make the organization more agile, responsive, and responsible when it comes to the maintenance of international peace and security. To properly seize this momentum, we need to consider the most feasible options and apply them gradually, starting with the GA decision on enlargement and additional elected seat allocation for regional groups. We noticed convergence on this, and we need to consider a clear, simple enlargement process, extending the number of seats for each underrepresented regional group— African, East European, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and the Caribbean.

Preserving rotation and accountability.

This would imply amending Article 23(1) 23(1) of the Charter and working with its secondary criteria related to equitable geographical distribution, which doesn't override the primary criteria, the contribution of new members to the maintenance of international peace and security. This could then be followed in a few years by a broader review review conference as stipulated in Article 109 of the Charter. A review clause of 15 years seems to get traction as we need more accountability, not just amongst ourselves and within the UN, but first and foremost to the people counting on our decisions.

To follow this feasibility path and to achieve tangible results,—

we need to show strong political will and a constructive spirit, avoiding radical options such as banning the veto overall or extending it to new permanent members. While non-permanent members' addition would follow the current election procedure, assigning permanent membership for specific member states within the regional group would entail political and timing sensitivities and would increase divisions, not bridge them. Moreover, introducing new seats for political or cross-regional groups would just create confusion, duplication, and would not serve the equity principle we all— we are all searching for in this reform process. Introducing a new category of semi-permanent members would have a similar effect and would further affect democratization, accountability, and transparency without proving concrete added value to a consistent and impartial approach of the Security Council. Reviewing working methods to render the Security Council processes and its decision-making more efficient is the purview of the Security Council members.
Thank you.

However, one aspect of its work is key for shaping its public image and the legitimacy of UN as a key actor responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security, the veto power.

And we devoted many hours discussing its role, the impressive weight and responsibility it carries, but also how to better encourage self-restraint and apply accountability mechanisms— with correlated political costs.

While we already have a limitation embedded in the UN Charter, which is reflected in self-restraint, we should consider additional limitations or deterrents. Returning to the feasibility aspect of this reform, to conclude, it's worth reflecting that without consensus that would include P5 assurances of non-diluting powers, The Council risks further erosion of legitimacy. Increased transparency in the reports to the GA or a consistent application of voluntary veto norms could help build this momentum. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Romania for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste.

Co-chairs, Timor-Leste reiterates its sincere appreciation for your dedicated efforts in guiding this process and for presenting the revised co-chair elements paper. We align ourselves with the statement delivered on behalf of the L69 Group and wish to highlight some points in our national capacities as follows. First, with regard to the fixed regional seats framework, the proposal appears to introduce a category of membership that differs from the established understanding of both permanent and elected membership within the Security Council. While the seats would be allocated on a regional basis, the states occupying them would serve in their national capacity and remain subject to reelection.— This raises important questions regarding the nature of such seats, their accountability, their relationship to the region from which they derive, and their place within the existing architecture of the Charter. Second, the revised co-chair element paper suggests that progress towards a consolidated model is contingent upon first bridging mutually exclusive positions. Including through concepts such as fixed regional seat proposal. In our view, a consolidated model should be treated as the procedural instrument that enables next stage of negotiations to begin. It is not a selection among competing proposals. Rather, it should serve as a complete and accurately attributed record of both convergence and unresolved issues.
Thank you.

Divergence. Only once positions are assembled in a single text can Member States meaningfully engage in a compromise and begin text-based negotiations. Third, we appreciate the reflection of the aspiration of Small Island Developing States in the element paper presented for a rotating seat in the Council as one of points of convergence. Further discussion in this regard is needed, as noted in the paper. Finally, we wish to highlight that support among Member States for expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories constitutes, in our assessment, a majority position and should therefore be reflected accordingly. Timor-Leste remains committed to a Member States-driven process that builds on the progress already achieved thus far. I thank you, co-chairs.
I thank the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ecuador.

Senhoras co-facilitadores.

Co-chairs, I'm grateful for the presentation of the elements paper, and I recognize the work done to faithfully reflect the opinions expressed by member states. My delegation particularly values the— the efforts made to identify areas of convergence and to objectively reflect those areas where substantive differences remain. While the paper does reflect some progress, it also highlights that fundamental issues such as membership categories, the veto, and regional representation continue without a consensus-based solution. At the same time, and unlike previous exercises, The paper seeks to explore possible avenues to bring divergent positions closer together and to advance on the discussion of a potential consolidated model. In this context, my delegation takes note of the proposal on regional seats and subject to election and periodic review. The document also recognizes the nature of the divergences on the categories of membership and the veto. This should lead us to a simple but necessary discussion. After more than a decade of negotiations, it would be hard to progress if we continue to simply reiterate widely recognized ideas. That's why my delegation insists that priority should be to consolidate the pre-identified consensus. The principal areas of convergence include the expansion of the council, strengthening transparency, accountability of its methods of work, deepening the relationship between the council and the General Assembly, increasing representation for developing countries, correcting— and correcting regional imbalances that remain, particularly in Africa. These elements represent the most robust foundation for us to make further progress. The reform calls for commitment, flexibility, and the will to build bridges between different perspectives to ensure that the result enjoys the broadest possible political acceptance. As we approach the 81st session of the General Assembly, we must focus our efforts on transforming the consensus into specific steps forward. This is, we believe, the most realistic path to achieving the shared objective, which is a significant reform of the Security Council. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of El Salvador.

Muchas gracias, co-presidents. Thank you very much, co-chairs. El Salvador is grateful for the convening of this meeting of the IGN on Security Council reform. We are further grateful for the presentation of the revised paper on convergence— and divergences that reflects the understanding of the co-chairs regarding the current status of our discussions. We value the efforts made to include the most recent developments in the process, as well as the discussions held during the 80th session of the General Assembly. El Salvador welcomes the fact that the document continues to recognize the momentum generated by the Pact for the Future, as well as the central role of the IGN process as the legitimate inclusive member-state-led forum for Security Council reform in accordance with Decision 62/557 of the General Assembly. At the same time, we believe it's positive that the document recognized that any progress towards a consolidated model will first require bringing positions closer together in areas where there are profound divergences. In this context, any future step should continue to be guided by the fundamental principles of the IJN, including the need to reach a solution that enjoys the most broadest possible political acceptance among member states. We take note of the proposals discussed during this session, including rich fixed regional seats.
